Mr. P. Jackson from WRc-NSF Ltd in the United Kingdom addressed practical aspects of chemicals. Dr. S. Ngowi from Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences in Tanzania provided input on pesticides. Dr. E.N. Ong from the National University of Singapore addressed emerging chemical hazards. Mr. O. Schmoll from the Federal Environment Agency in Germany worked on water safety plan capacity building and monitoring. Professor M. Callan from the National Health and Medical Research Council in Australia. Ms. C. Vickers and Dr. A. Tritscher facilitated important liaisons with international chemical risk assessment programs at WHO headquarters. Dr. M. Perez contributed on behalf of the Radiation and Environmental Health Programme at WHO headquarters. Dr. M. Zaim from the Pesticide Evaluation Scheme at WHO headquarters provided input on pesticides added to drinking water for public health purposes. The Coordinator of Water, Sanitation, Hygiene, and Health at WHO headquarters (formerly Jamie Bartram and, since 2009, Robert Bos) provided strategic direction throughout the process. For updates to the fourth edition of the guidelines, contributions were made by experts in the Guideline Development Group or working groups on chemical, microbial, or protection and control topics. The development of the guidelines involved contributions from numerous individuals across various countries. Their efforts, particularly those who provided peer or public domain review comments, are greatly appreciated. Financial and technical support from several organizations is also acknowledged, including the Agence Française de Développement (France), the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Australia), the Federal Environment Agency (Germany), Health Canada, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (Japan), the Ministry of Environment and Water Resources (Singapore), the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs (Luxembourg), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Netherlands), the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, the United Kingdom Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, and the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The guidelines for drinking-water quality aim to protect public health by providing recommendations for managing risks from hazards that may compromise the safety of drinking water. These recommendations should be considered in the context of managing risks from other sources of exposure, such as waste, air, food, and consumer products. Water is essential for life, and a satisfactory supply of safe, accessible drinking water must be available to all. Improving access to safe drinking water can yield significant health benefits. Every effort should be made to achieve drinking water that is as safe as practicable. Safe drinking water, as defined by the guidelines, poses no significant health risk over a lifetime of consumption, including for individuals with varying sensitivities across life stages. Those at greatest risk of waterborne disease include infants, young children, the elderly, and individuals with weakened health, particularly in unsanitary conditions. People at risk of waterborne illness may need to take additional precautions, such as boiling their drinking water. Safe drinking water is required for all domestic purposes, including drinking, food preparation, and personal hygiene. The guidelines also apply to packaged water and ice intended for human consumption. However, higher-quality water may be necessary for specific purposes, such as renal dialysis, cleaning contact lenses, or certain food production and pharmaceutical uses. The guidelines are intended to support the development and implementation of risk management strategies to ensure the safety of drinking water supplies by controlling hazardous constituents. These strategies may include national or regional standards based on the scientific foundation provided in the guidelines. The guidelines describe minimum requirements for safe practices to protect consumer health and derive numerical guideline values for water constituents or indicators of water quality. When defining mandatory limits, it is preferable to consider the guidelines in the context of local or national environmental, social, economic, and cultural conditions. The guidelines should also be part of an overall health protection strategy that includes sanitation and other measures, such as managing food contamination. The guidelines promote an integrated preventive management framework for safety, applied from the water source to the consumer. This approach involves systematic risk assessment and management throughout the drinking water supply chain, from catchment and source water to the consumer. It includes identifying ways to manage risks and ensuring that control measures are effective. The guidelines provide a scientific basis for national authorities to develop drinking water regulations and standards appropriate for their specific national context.
